2 Table of Contents Introduction 2 Background 3 Getting Started 4 Implementation Checklist for the National CLAS Standards 5-7 Your Organization’s CLAS Action Worksheet 8 CLAS Testimonials from Organizational Leaders 9-11 Introduction Culturally and linguistically appropriate services (CLAS) are increasingly recognized as effective in improving quality of care because they help organizations address the cultural and communication barriers that many individuals face when seeking services. In 2015, the Office of Minority Health at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) conducted a study to better understand how organizations use the National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Services in Health and Health Care (the National CLAS Standards). In this document, you will learn what we learned. The checklist of implementation practices lists successful CLAS-related organizational activities we observed across the organizations we studied. We provide a CLAS action worksheet for you to plan CLAS activities at your office or organization or other type of health care services. At the end of this document, testimonials from those who participated in our 2015 study are included, to give you a snapshot at how and why to implement the National CLAS Standards.

3 Background What is CLAS? CLAS stands for culturally and linguistically appropriate services. CLAS is services that are respectful of and responsive to each person’s culture and communication needs. CLAS helps your organization take into account cultural health beliefs, preferred languages, health literacy levels, and communication needs. What are the National CLAS Standards? The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services in Health and Health Care (the National CLAS Standards) gives health organizations 15 action steps for providing CLAS. The National CLAS Standards and information to help you put them into practice may be found at www.ThinkCulturalHealth.hhs.gov. The Principal Standard (No. 1) calls on organizations to “provide effective, equitable, understandable and respectful quality care and services that are responsive to diverse cultural health beliefs and practices, preferred languages, health literacy, and other communication needs.” The remaining standards are divided into three themes: 1. Governance, Leadership, and Workforce (Standards 2‐4); 2. Communication and Language Assistance (Standards 5‐8); and 3. Engagement, Continuous Improvement, and Accountability (Standards 9‐15). The National CLAS Standards can be applied to a wide array of professions and sectors, including medical care, behavioral health, public health, social work, community health, emergency health, and more. The HHS Office of Minority Health developed the Standards to advance health equity, improve quality of services, and help eliminate disparities. The Standards were first published in 2000 and updated in 2013. The National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services in Health and Health Care: A Blueprint for Advancing and Sustaining CLAS Policy and Practice, commonly referred to as The Blueprint, provides an in‐depth explanation of, and implementation strategies for, each of the National CLAS Standards. There is no single correct way to implement the National CLAS Standards. Your organization may decide to implement some but not all of them, or your organization may wish to implement some sooner than others. After deciding which standards to implement, you can refer to The Blueprint for ideas to get started.

Getting Started Who is filling this out? 4 Name Role or Title Department or Division Organization How to use the implementation checklist The checklist is divided into practices that relate to each Theme and Standard of the National CLAS Standards. We suggest that you review the checklist and, for each practice, select whether your organization is currently implementing it, planning to implement it, or not planning to implement it at this time. Each practice is numbered according to the Theme and Standard it corresponds to. For example, 1.2 corresponds to Theme 1, Standard 2. You may find that some practices are not feasible for or relevant to your organization right now, or you may be unsure whether your organization is implementing a certain practice. That’s okay. This checklist is simply meant to guide your and your organization’s efforts to better provide CLAS. As you go through the checklist, you may find it helpful to refer to The Blueprint, although it is not necessary to do so to fill out the checklist.

5 Theme 1: Governance, Leadership, and Workforce Checklist of National CLAS Standards Implementation Practices Select your organization’s stage of implemention for each practice Currently implementing Planning to implement Not planning to implement at this time Identify and designate a CLAS champion or champions, who are supported by the organization’s leadership, and whose specific responsibilities include (at a minimum) continuous learning about, promoting, and identifying and sharing educational resources about CLAS and the National CLAS Standards throughout the organization. Create and implement a formal CLAS implementation plan that is (at a minimum) endorsed and supported by the organization’s leadership, that describes how each Standard is understood, how each Standard will be implemented and assessed, and who in the organization is responsible for overseeing implementation. Target recruitment efforts to the populations served to increase the recruitment of culturally and linguistically diverse individuals, through actions such as: posting job descriptions in multiple languages in local community media, holding job fairs in the community(ies) served, and/or working with leaders of local community institutions to create mentorship and training programs targeting populations served. Create internal organizational mentorship programs, specifically targeting culturally and linguistically diverse individuals, that provide information about and support for additional training opportunities, and that links individuals in junior positions with individuals in senior positions to receive career guidance and advice. Deliver or make freely available continuous CLAS-related training and technical assistance to leadership and all staff. Create and disseminate new resources about CLAS within the organization using widely accessible platforms (e.g., employee- dedicated webpages, employee Intranet, employee break room). Incorporate assessment of CLAS competencies (e.g., bilingual communication, cross-cultural communication, cultural and linguistic knowledge) on an ongoing basis into staff performance ratings. 1.2a 1.2b 1.3a 1.3b 1.4a 1.4b 1.4c

6 Theme 2: Communication and Language Assistance Checklist of National CLAS Standards Implementation Practices Select your organization’s stage of implemention for each practice Currently implementing Planning to implement Not planning to implement at this time Complete an organizational assessment specific to language assistance services to describe existing language assistance services and to determine how they can be more effective and efficient. Standardize procedures for staff members and train staff in those procedures. It may be appropriate to provide staff with a script to ensure that they inform individuals of the availability of language assistance and to inquire whether they will need to utilize any of the available services. Provide individuals with notification that describes what communication and language assistance is available, in what languages the assistance is available, and to whom they are available. Notification should clearly state that communication and language assistance is provided by the organization free of charge to individuals. Require that all individuals serving as interpreters complete certification or other formal assessments of linguistic and health care terminology skills to demonstrate competency. Provide financial and/or human resource (e.g., time off) incentives to staff who complete interpreter training and meet assessment criteria, to build organizational capacity to provide competent language assistance. Formalize processes for translating materials into languages other than English and for evaluating the quality of these translations. This may include testing materials with target audiences. 2.5a 2.5b 2.6 2.7b 2.7a 2.8

7 Theme 3: Engagement, Continuous Improvement, and Accountability Checklist of National CLAS Standards Implementation Practices Select your organization’s stage of implemention for each practice Incorporate CLAS into mission, vision, and/or strategic plans by determining how organization acknowledges and addresses concepts such as diversity, equity, inclusion, and practices such as asking individuals about preferences for care/services. Currently implementing Planning to implement Not planning to implement at this time Tailor existing evaluation efforts to include measures of CLAS implementation (e.g., patient/client satisfaction measures can include questions about CLAS; outcome data can be stratified by REAL data to determine demographic differences). Complete a CLAS-related organizational assessment of the cultural and linguistic needs of populations served and of organizational resources to address these needs. Collect race, ethnicity, and language (REAL) data (at a minimum) from all individuals receiving services, either by tailoring existing data collection approaches or creating a new data collection process. Use REAL data to identify needs, describe current care and service provision trends, and improve care and service provision. Collaborate with stakeholders and community members in community health needs assessment data collection, analysis, and reporting efforts to increase data reliability and validity. Include community members in the process of planning programs and developing policies to ensure cultural and linguistic appropriateness by convening town hall meetings, conducting focus groups, and/or creating community advisory groups. Consider using staff as cultural brokers to help improve feedback mechanisms, conflict resolution process, and communication with culturally and linguistically diverse individuals. Partner with community organizations to lead discussions about the services provided and progress made and to create advisory boards on issues affecting diverse populations and how best to serve and reach them. 3.9 3.10a 3.10b 3.11a 3.11b 3.12 3.13 3.14 3.15

8 Your CLAS Action Worksheet Review the practices you checked as “planning to implement. ” We suggest choosing three practices that your organization or department will focus on implementing next. Write these three practices down, along with timeframes for their implementation. How will you help your organization implement these National CLAS Standards? Write down a few concrete action steps. Consider your objectives, challenges, and staff and resources that can support you. Congratulations! You now have a CLAS implementation action plan!

ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 7 Thank you for taking the time to review and use the ADSA Engagement Guide. This guide was developed from our collective, learned experience in community engagement and is intended for all Aging and Disability Services Administration (ADSA) staff members in the Department of Human Services (DHS). The purpose of this document is to help ADSA staff members plan and implement engagement efforts with external partners including individuals, groups or teams, agencies, counties, Tribal Nations, organizations or other entities outside of ADSA. It prioritizes the evolving needs of a community one project at a time by getting affected them involved during the planning process in a meaningful way. Also, this guide will help streamline outreach and engagement processes and practices across the administration while helping to make sure these efforts are equitable and appropriate. Communities have valuable knowledge and wisdom about their own needs. As an agency responsible for developing policies and procedures aimed at meeting a person’s basic needs, authentic community engagement is essential to improve DHS services and achieve equitable outcomes. We share a responsibility to build and maintain relationships with communities and other partners. Each person in this administration plays a role in this, even though we have our own functions and responsibilities. We recognize that effective community engagement requires the creation of processes, practices and systems that reflect how a community wants to be engaged and supports cooperation. For this reason, we want to include insights, feedback and recommendations from our external partners in future versions of this guide. Leverage existing DHS sources This guide pulls together relevant information from many existing DHS sources to improve and expand community engagement. For more information, go to Appendix A – Existing resources. 1. The DHS Community Relations’ Community Engagement Guide (PDF) is an agencywide resource that staff members can use by to organize meaningful and intentional community engagement activities. This guide provides a detailed framework of effective community engagement at DHS including definitions, principles, values and best practices. 2. The equity analysis process is grounded in the assumption that a community engages in the planning, implementation and evaluation of DHS programs and initiatives. The equity analysis process is an umbrella term describing the steps and actions used to assess disparate impacts on different populations and groups. 3. ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 12 Our shared responsibility for community engagement Engagement is critical when a decision, policy, practice, program or service will affect or impact people’s lives – especially those who have been historically excluded or underserved. Whether your role involves policymaking, research and evaluation, grant-making, program delivery, hiring or other areas, engagement will likely be a part of your work. The following list gives you an idea when it would be appropriate to incorporate engagement into your plans. 1. When a decision affects how people live, work, access services or experience their community. 2. When there are equity implications – it affects or impacts different groups differently, often negatively. 3. When buy-in or long-term success is needed, like implementing policies, delivering programs or services, improving systems or processes, testing new initiatives, etc. 4. When you have limited information and insight into the lived experiences of the people affected, do not assume. Instead, engage communities and partners. The following list provides you with examples of areas where engagement is crucial or beneficial. 1. Designing or managing grant-making processes, including requests for information (RFIs), requests for proposals (RFPs) and selecting grantees. 2. Gathering public comment and input, like feedback on new assessments and assessment processes, funding decisions or preferred engagement methods. 3. Conducting research and evaluation, performance and accountability, fiscal analysis and reporting, including designing, proposing, implementing, monitoring and reporting on studies, evaluations, policies, practices, budgets, programs or services. 4. Recruiting and procuring contractors or vendors for grants, research, evaluations, professional development or other partnership activities. 5. Recruiting for positions, including internships and employment with DHS. Engagement activators Examples of engagement areas

ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 13 As you start planning, it is helpful to acknowledge that engagement is not linear. It is common to adjust along the way. So, be flexible. Remember, a successful engagement plan for one project may not necessarily mean it will work effectively for another one. Consideration 1: Know the importance of trust, relationships and accountability As staff working in human services, we are often tasked with engaging communities to provide support, resources and care. It is important to recognize that for many historically underserved communities — people with disabilities, communities of color, low-income populations, refugees and immigrants, LGBTQIA2S+ communities, Tribal Nations and American Indian communities to name a few — there is a long history of mistrust toward government institutions. The mistrust is rooted in lived experiences of systemic discrimination, forced removals, surveillance, underinvestment and policies that have caused real, lasting harm. Even well-intentioned programs have sometimes failed to involve communities in meaningful ways or unintentionally reinforce inequities. Engagement is not just about outreach. It is about (re)building trust, being accountable, being present and showing up consistently with humility, transparency and a willingness to listen. Additionally, engagement is about centering community voices and wisdom and acting on what communities say they need when it comes to designing/implementing programs and policies as well as using that information for decision-making at every step. When we engage with a community and when there is transparency in decision-making, it fosters trust and demonstrates accountability. This helps build lasting relationships. ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 14 Throughout this work, reflect on these questions: 1. What assumptions do you have about the community/partner, and are you prepared to challenge them? 2. What are helpful ways in which you can be supported to address potential assumptions and bias? 3. Are you and other staff members ready to engage in a way that will build relationships and trust with the community? 4. Do staff members have the appropriate knowledge, training or expertise to authentically engage? Consideration 2: Define the purpose, roles and resources for engagement Community engagement should be intentional, meaningful and purposeful. It should not be done simply for the sake of doing it (i.e., checking the box). Start planning by having a clear understanding of what will be done and how information and learnings from your engagement activities will be used. 1. Understand what this work entails by answering these questions: a. Why do you want to engage with communities or partners on a particular issue or with certain groups — what is the purpose and what are your goals? b. What are your initial expectations and what do you hope to learn from this? c. How do you plan to use the information and learnings from your engagement activities? d. What resources are available to you — funding and compensation, staffing, staff capacity, etc.? e. How, if at all, might staff capacity be affected by the timeline and vice versa? How will the timeline affect engagement with various communities/partners? f. Who is responsible for leading, planning, coordinating, supporting and implementing engagement activities? g. What potential challenges or barriers might you face in planning, coordinating and executing the engagement activities, and how you plan to address them? Understanding context is essential. It is helpful to obtain as much background information and context (both historical and current) as necessary for the type of engagement you hope to conduct. Network with individuals in the agency to learn more about what information is available. 1. What existing data and information, if any, do you have that can tell us about the issue or topic at hand? Who does this issue or topic affect or impact? What populations, if any, are disproportionately impacted? Have these been positive or negative? 2. How, if at all, can the data and information help to inform engagement? 3. How, if at all, have communities or partners provided us with feedback in the past/from past projects? Where can we find this information and is this information still relevant? 4. What gaps, if any, still exist in the data and information you have? 5. What current events, including the political climate, is impacting and/or will impact engagement efforts? How can we engage communities, ensuring their safety and trust?

ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 15 Consideration 3: Include multiple perspectives You are encouraged to work with internal and external communities and partners to develop and implement your engagement plan. Although this may require more time, effort and work, the most effective engagement plans are often done in consultation, collaboration and/or co-created with others. It is best practice to consult with individuals or teams who can provide feedback, input and insights to accomplish your engagement goals. Consultations are a great way to identify potential collaboration opportunities. Helpful tips for collaborating with others 1. Consider using participatory or InfoLink – Person-centered approaches/DHS – Person- centered practices which include human-centered design, design thinking, person- centered planning, customer experience, qualitative research, plain language, to name a few. 2. Involve communities and partners from the beginning. We have a wealth of knowledge and resources that we can tap into. Communities and partners often serve as a key resource to identify best strategies for outreach and engagement and help us make connections. Identify who the collaborating partners are and determine what kind of collaboration you are looking for. Are you seeking a particular partnership, consultation or is there another purpose? 3. Be clear and transparent with your partners about the decision-making process such as when and how you want input, who makes decisions on what, etc. 4. Find lessons from past engagement efforts to help design your engagement plan. 5. Ask team members as well as your supervisors and directors for information on existing projects so you can streamline engagement efforts. Consultation

Stat. §10.65, Tribal consultation is “a formal engagement between agency official and the governing body or bodies of an individual Minnesota Tribal government that the agency or an individual Tribal government may initiate.” This is a structured process controlled exclusively by the Office of Tribal and Urban Indian Relations for all “matters that have Tribal implications.” If your department is proposing a change that will impact Tribes, you need to consider Tribal consultation. Contact the Office of Tribal and Urban Indian Relations early in the process to find out when this consultation needs to be done. For more information and resources, visit DHS – Office of Tribal and Urban Indian Relations. Contact: For more information, email Office of Tribal and Urban Indian Relations. Make the most of remaining vision Many people who are deafblind have some residual vision. You may find these simple strategies helpful: • Choose a well-lit space. Ask the person if the lighting is acceptable or should be adjusted. • Make sure the light is shining on you, not in the person’s eyes. • Sit close enough for the person to see your face. • Do not stand or sit in front of a bright window or light. This may make it difficult for a person with limited vision to see your hands, lips or facial expression. • Wear solid-colored clothing that contrasts with your skin tone. If you have lighter skin, wear dark clothing; if you have darker skin, wear a lighter color. This will make it easier for a person with limited vision to follow ASL signs, gestures and focus on your face. • Identify yourself. • Say the person’s name when speaking to that person in a group situation. Make the most of remaining hearing • Do not assume that the person can hear and understand you just because they are wearing a hearing aid. Ask the person what you can do to make communications easier. Remember, they are the expert! • Eliminate background noise as much as possible. Close the door. Turn off the television. Ask for a table in a less crowded area of a restaurant, workplace or social gathering. • Ask the person where they would like to sit. This allows them to control their environment as much as possible. • Look directly at the person. Maintain eye contact and do not cover your mouth, eat or chew gum while you are talking. • Speak clearly, slowly, and loudly but do not shout. • If the person does not understand you, rephrase your message. Stick to one idea at a time. • Try to keep your sentences short and to the point. • Use gestures, facial expressions and other kinds of nonverbal communication to help get your message across. • Get the person’s attention before you start talking. If the person has some residual hearing, you can say the person’s name. Otherwise, tap the person on the shoulder or knock on the table. Wait until the person acknowledges you or makes eye contact before you begin. • Check in with the person to be sure that they understand what is being discussed. • Allow time for the person to respond. Do not rush to fill the silence.

Because of this, we all have used non-inclusive language at times. 1. Minnesota Olmstead Implementation Office’s (OIO) Inclusive Language Guide (for internal staff only): This guide was developed by OIO. The purpose of this guide is not meant to shame, but to offer the opportunity to learn and alternative substitutes to common language. For questions or to share feedback, email OIO. 2. Pronouns: Pronouns are as specific as names. Using someone’s correct pronouns shows respect, affirms their identity and creates an inclusive environment. Avoid assuming a person’s pronoun or gender. Two-spirit identities: A term reflecting traditional Indigenous/Aboriginal worldviews around gender diversity and fluidity. The term is used by many Indigenous or Aboriginal peoples in North America and describes a broad range of roles that can span or add nuances to distinctions between gender, sex and sexuality. What happened to our ancestors? 1. 1634: The first Native American mission school was established in 1634. Andrew White, a Jesuit missionary, established a mission school in what is now Southern Maryland. He said the purpose of the mission school was "to extend civilization and instruction to this ignorant race and show them the way to heaven.” 2. 1830: The Indian Removal Act was authorized in 1830 which allowed the president to negotiate treaties to remove the remaining Eastern Native Americans to lands west of the Mississippi. Under Presidents Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren, most of the Tribes remaining east of the Mississippi were removed in a series of migrations, some voluntary and some forced. ADSA Outreach and Engagement Guide | 53 3. 1851: Through the Treaty of Traverse des Sioux and the Treaty of Mendota, the Mdewakanton and Wahpekute bands of the Lower Sioux ceded territory of nearly 24 million acres of land. The U.S. paid the Dakota an annuity the equivalent of $0.075 an acre and charged settlers $1.25 an acre. The US set aside two reservations for the Sioux along the Minnesota River, each about 20 miles wide and 70 miles long. Later the government declared these were intended to be temporary, to force the Sioux out of Minnesota. 4. 1862: The Dakota war of 1862 began when the Dakota, who were facing starvation and displacement, attacked white settlements at the Lower Sioux Agency in southwest Minnesota. A crop failure in 1861, followed by a harsh winter along with poor hunting due to depletion of wild game, led to starvation and severe hardship for the eastern Dakota. Although payments were guaranteed, the U.S. government was two months behind on both money and food. The war lasted for five weeks and in the aftermath, the Dakota people were exiled from their homelands, forcibly sent to reservations in the Dakotas and Nebraska, and the State of Minnesota confiscated and sold all their remaining land in the state. The war also ended with the largest mass execution in United States history with the hanging of 38 Dakota men. 5. 1887: In Minnesota, the first Indian boarding school opened in Morris. In total, there were 15 schools of this type throughout the state. Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian school, stated of his philosophy of Indian Boarding schools, “kill the Indian in him and save the man.” 6. 1889: The Nelson Act was passed which mandated allotting communal Indian lands to individual households in Indian Country and selling the surplus. The goal of the Nelson Act was to consolidate Native Americans within the state of Minnesota on a western reservation and, secondly, to encourage allotment of communal lands to individual households to encourage subsistence farming and assimilation. 7. 1978: 350 years after the first boarding school opened, the American Indian Religious Freedom Act was enacted to return basic civil liberties to Native Americans, and to allow them to practice, protect and preserve their inherent right of freedom to believe, express, and exercise their traditional religious rites, spiritual and cultural practices. These rights also included access to sacred sites, freedom to worship through traditional ceremonial rites and the possession/use of objects traditionally considered sacred by their respective cultures. 8. 2022: The Indian Child Welfare (ICWA) is challenged in the Supreme Court. The ICWA held jurisdiction over the removal of Native American (Indian) children from their families in custody, foster care and adoption cases. It gives Tribal governments exclusive power over children who reside on or are domiciled on a reservation. Some distinctions include: 1. In North America, the collective terms “Native American” and “Native North American” are acceptable (and may be preferred to “American Indian”). The term “Native American” became widespread in the U.S. during the civil rights movement in the 1960s and 1970s and the self- determination era. These terms are also commonly used in government. “Indian” usually refers to people from India. Specify the nation or people if possible (e.g., Cherokee, Navajo, Sioux). 2. Hawaiian Natives may identify as “Native American,” “Hawaiian Native,” “Indigenous Peoples of the Hawaiian Islands” and/or “Pacific Islander.” 3. In Canada, refer to the Indigenous people collectively as “Indigenous Peoples” or “Aboriginal Peoples” (National Aboriginal Health Organization, n.d.); specify the nation or people if possible (e.g., People of the First Nations of Canada, People of the First Nations or First Nations People; Métis; Inuit). 4. In Alaska, the Indigenous people may identify as “Alaska Natives.” The Indigenous people in Alaska, Canada, Siberia and Greenland may identify as a specific nation (e.g., Inuit, Iñupiat). Avoid the term “Eskimo” because it may be considered pejorative. 5. In Latin America and the Caribbean, refer to the Indigenous people collectively as “Indigenous Peoples” and by name if possible (e.g., Quechua, Aymara, Taíno, Nahuatl). 6. In Australia, the Indigenous people may identify as “Aboriginal People” or “Aboriginal Australians” and “Torres Strait Islander People” or “Torres Strait Island Australians.” Refer to specific groups when people use these terms to refer to themselves (e.g., Anangu Pitjantjatjara, Arrernte). 7.
